summary.en: Create a text alternative for visual and auditory content. Non-text information is available to more people. People who can’t fully see or hear content can understand it.

examples.good: Products page

note.en: Good: Combining adjacent image and text links for the same resource (H2).
Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 1.1.1 due to conveying information exclusively using CSS background images (F3).

title.fr: Contenus seulement audio et seulement vidéo (pré-enregistrés)

summary.en: Provide an alternative when content is perceivable with only one sense. Audio and video-only content can be understood by more people. People who can’t fully see or hear content can understand it.

examples.good: Audio description of "Mars Landing"

note.en: Good: Providing audio that describes the important video content and describing it as such (G166).

summary.en: Provide synchronized text for audio content in existing videos. Videos can be played with captions. People who are deaf or hard of hearing can understand audio in videos.

examples.good:
<video poster="myvideo.png" controls>
  <source src="myvideo.mp4" srclang="en" type="video/mp4">
  <track kind="captions" label="English" src="myvideo_en.vtt" srclang="en">
</video>

note.en: Good: Using the track element to provide captions (H95).

title.fr: Audio-description ou version de remplacement pour un média temporel (pré-enregistré)

summary.en: Provide a description of the visual content in videos. Prerecorded videos can be understood by more people. People who are blind or who cannot understand the visual content can have it described.

note.en: Good: Using the body of the object element (H53).

summary.en: Provide synchronized text for audio content in real-time videos. Live videos have captions. People who are deaf or hard of hearing can understand audio in real-time video content.

Provide a synchronized spoken description of the visual content in videos. Videos can be played with audio descriptions. People who cannot see or understand the visual content can hear about it while playing videos.

Use code to reinforce relationships and information conveyed through presentation. Information about content structure is available to more people. People can adapt the presentation to suit their needs while preserving the original meaning.

examples.bad:
<style>
.heading1{
  font-family: Times, serif;
  font-size:200%;
  font-weight:bold;
}
</style>
examples.good: ... What she really meant to say was, "This is not OK, it is excellent"! ...

note.en: Good: Using semantic markup to mark emphasized or special text (H49). Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 1.3.1 due to using changes in text presentation to convey information without using the appropriate markup or text (F2).

summary.en: Use code to preserve meaningful content order. The order of content can be understood by more people. Assistive technology can present content to users in the proper order.

examples.bad:
W e l c o m e

  can also be used to add white space, producing similar failures:

H E L L O
examples.good: The title says "פעילות הבינאום, W3C" in Hebrew.

note.en: Good: Using the dir attribute on an inline element to resolve problems with nested directional runs (H56). Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 1.3.2 due to using white space characters to control spacing within a word (F32).

summary.en: Describe controls by name, not just by appearance or location. Instructions are understandable by more people. People who are blind or have low vision need non-visual instructions.

examples.good:
Sign up to our mailing list

Complete the form and then press the lower-right (sign up) button.

note.en: Good: Providing textual identification of items that otherwise rely only on sensory information to be understood (G96).

summary.en: Don't lock content to either portrait or landscape presentation. Devices can be used in any orientation. Wheelchair users and others may have devices mounted in a fixed orientation.

examples.bad:
<style>
/* Orientation "door slam" Styling */

@media all and (orientation: landscape) {
  .rotate { display: block; }
  .content { display: none; }
}

@media all and (orientation: portrait) {
  .rotate { display: none; }
  .content { display: block; }
}

.rotate {
  text-align: center;
  font-size: 2rem;
  margin-top: 4rem;
}
</style>

note.en: Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 1.3.4 due to showing a message asking to reorient device (F100).

title.fr: Identifier la finalité de la saisie

summary.en: Use code to indicate the purpose of common inputs, where technology allows. It is easier to fill out forms. Some people with cognitive disabilities may not understand the input's purpose from the label alone.

note.en: Good: Using HTML autocomplete attributes (H98).

summary.en: Use information in addition to color, such as shape or text, to convey meaning. Color is not the only way of distinguishing information. Not everyone sees colors or sees them the same way.

examples.bad: There are many resources to find out more about the rain in Spain.
examples.good:
<style>
  .required {
    color:#ec0000;
  }
</style>
<label for="lastname" class="required">Last name (required):</label>
<input autocomplete="family-name" id="lastname" type="text" value="">

note.en: Good: Including a text cue for colored form control labels (G205). Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 1.4.1 due to creating links that are not visually evident without color vision (F73).

summary.en: If you play audio content automatically, let people turn it down or off. A page that plays music or sounds doesn't disrupt people. Sound distracts some people, and also interferes with screen readers.
Provide sufficient contrast between text and its background. Text can be seen by more people. Some people cannot read faint text.

examples.bad: My background is white.

note.en: Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 1.4.3, 1.4.6 and 1.4.8 due to specifying foreground colors without specifying background colors or vice versa (F24).

summary.en: Ensure text can be doubled in size. Text can be enlarged. Some people can only read text when it is bigger.

examples.good:
#nav_menu { width: 20em; height: 100em; }
#nav_list { font-size: 100%; }

note.en: Good: Specifying the size of text containers using em units (C28).

examples.bad:
Now is the time for all good men to come to the aid of their country.

The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.

note.en: Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 1.4.4 when resizing visually rendered text up to 200 percent causes the text, image or controls to be clipped, truncated or obscured (F69).

summary.en: Use text instead of pictures of text. Users can adjust how text is presented. People cannot alter how text looks in images.

examples.good: The JavaScript method to convert a string to uppercase is toUpperCase().

note.en: Good: Using CSS to control visual presentation of text (C22).

summary.en: Make lines of text reflow within the viewport. Content can be enlarged without increasing line length. People who need bigger text find it difficult if they must scroll to read long lines.

examples.good:
...
... ...
...
...
...
...

note.en: Good: Using media queries and grid CSS to reflow columns (C32).

summary.en: Ensure meaningful visual cues achieve 3:1 against the background. Important visual information meets the same minimum contrast required for larger text. Some people cannot see elements with low contrast.

examples.bad: :focus {outline: none}

note.en: Good: Creating a two-color focus indicator to ensure sufficient contrast with all components (C40). Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 1.4.11, 2.4.7 and 2.4.13 due to styling element outlines and borders in a way that removes or renders non-visible the visual focus indicator (F78).

summary.en: Users can adjust text spacing to make it easier to read. Some people need text with different spacing or font characteristics.

examples.bad:
Now is the time for all good men to come to the aid of their country.

The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
examples.good:
<style>
/* CSS: No height property is set.*/
</style>

note.en: Good: Allowing for text spacing override (C36). Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 1.4.12 due to clipped or overlapped content when text spacing is adjusted (F104).

title.fr: Contenu au survol ou au focus

summary.en: If hover or focus causes content changes, ensure interaction is predictable. More users can perceive and dismiss non-persistent content. Unpredictable temporary content can be hard for some to consume and may disrupt others.

examples.good: This is the trigger And this additional text gives additional context on the trigger term . Text and popup are in one link (a) element.

note.en: Good: Making content on focus or hover hoverable, dismissible, and persistent (SCR39).

summary.en: Ensure pointer actions have a keyboard equivalent. Everything can be done with a keyboard except freehand movements. Many people rely on the keyboard interface, including blind and some mobility impaired people.

examples.good: Example Site

note.en: Good: Using HTML form controls and links (H91). Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 2.1.1 due to using only pointing-device-specific event handlers (including gesture) for a function (F54).

summary.en: Ensure users always know how to navigate away from components. Keyboard users don't get stuck. People who rely on the keyboard often have no other means to navigate.

Ensure character-only shortcut keys can be turned off or modified. Reduce accidental activation of keyboard shortcuts. Character-key shortcuts are easy to accidentally trigger, especially with speech input.
Let users turn off, adjust, or extend time limits. Users have adequate time to complete tasks. People with disabilities may need more time to complete activities.

examples.bad: If your browser supports Refresh, you'll be transported to our new site in 5 seconds, otherwise select the link manually.
examples.good:
Stock Market Quotes

...

note.en: Good: Providing a script that warns the user a time limit is about to expire (SCR16). Bad: Failure due to using meta redirect with a time limit (F40).

summary.en: Let users control content changes that occur in parallel with other content. Fewer users are distracted by content that updates or moves. Some people with cognitive disabilities and attention deficits are distracted by continuous movement.

examples.bad:
<script>
  // blink "on" state
  function show(){
      document.getElementById("blink1").style.visibility = "visible";
      window.setTimeout(hide, 450);
   }
    
   // blink "off" state
   function hide(){
      document.getElementById("blink1").style.visibility = "hidden";
      window.setTimeout(show, 450);
   }

   // kick it off
   show();
</script>
examples.good:
...

This text will scroll and a Pause/Scroll link will be present when JavaScript and CSS are supported and active.

...

note.en: Good: Using script to scroll content, and providing a mechanism to pause it (SCR33). Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 2.2.2 due to a script that causes a blink effect without a mechanism to stop the blinking at 5 seconds or less (F50).

title.fr: Pas plus de trois flashs ou sous le seuil critique

summary.en: Avoid content that flashes, or keep it under thresholds. Content does not trigger seizures. Flashing content can cause migraines, dizziness, nausea, and seizures.
Provide a means of skipping repeating content. Users can more easily navigate by keyboard. Users reliant on the keyboard interface can move around pages efficiently.

examples.good:
Search Technical Periodicals

Search

Available Periodicals

  • Professional Coder
  • Algorithms
  • Journal of Software Engineering

Search Results

... search results are returned in this section ...

note.en: Good: Providing heading elements at the beginning of each section of content (H69).

summary.en: Provide a descriptive page title using appropriate technology. Each web page has a meaningful title. Page titles help users identify and distinguish different pages.

examples.good:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>The World Wide Web Consortium</title>     
  </head>
  <body>
      ...   
  </body> 
</html>

note.en: Good: Providing a title using the title element (H25).

summary.en: Elements receive focus in an order that preserves meaning. Keyboard users navigate content in a correct order. Navigating a site or application with only the keyboard will make sense.

examples.bad:
1. Homepage
  2. Chapter 1
  3. Chapter 2
  4. Chapter 3
examples.good:
All The News About Turbo Encabulators

Sign up to our mailing list

All form fields are required.

note.en: Good: Creating modal dialogs with the HTML dialog element (H102). Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 2.4.3 due to using tabindex to create a tab order that does not preserve meaning and operability (F44).

summary.en: Provide descriptive names or context for all links. Users understand what each link will do. People with visual and cognitive disabilities can navigate more easily.

examples.bad:
A British businessman has racked up 2 million flyer miles and plans to travel on the world's first commercial tourism flights to space.

Read More...
examples.good: Current routes at Boulders Climbing Gym

note.en: Good: Providing link text that describes the purpose of a link for anchor elements (H30). Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 2.4.4 due to providing link context only in content that is not related to the link (F63).

summary.en: Provide at least two options for reaching the same content. Users can get to content in multiple ways. Not everyone can navigate content in the same way.
Provide descriptive headings and labels A page's content is described in headings and labels People can orient themselves, especially those with cognitive or visual disabilities.

examples.good:
Disaster preparation

Flood preparation

Fire preparation

note.en: Good: Providing descriptive headings (G130).

summary.en: Ensure each item receiving focus has a visible indicator. Users know which element has keyboard focus. Without a focus indicator, sighted keyboard users cannot operate the page.

examples.bad: <input type="submit" onFocus="this.blur();">
examples.good:
• Home
  • Services
  • Projects
  • Demos
  • About us
  • Contact us
  • Links

note.en: Good: Using CSS to change the presentation of a user interface component when it receives focus (C15). Bad: Failure of Success Criteria 2.1.1, 2.4.7, 2.4.13, and 3.2.1 due to using script to remove focus when focus is received (F55).

summary.en: Ensure when an item gets keyboard focus, it is at least partially visible. Keep the focused item visible. People who can't use a mouse need to see what has keyboard focus.

examples.good:
Fixed-Position Banner

Header Content

Main Content

Sidebar Content

Here's an example link in the sidebar.

Footer Content

Here's an example link in the footer.

note.en: Good: Using CSS scroll-padding to un-obscure content (C43).

title.fr: Gestes pour le contrôle du pointeur

summary.en: Provide single-point operation for all functions. Let users operate touchscreens with one finger and reduced gestures. Not everyone can perform complex and multi-touch gestures.
Make pointer cancellation predictable and consistent. Reduce accidental activation of controls by mouse or touch. Make it easier for anyone to recover from something they didn’t mean to do.

examples.bad:
<!-- modal dialog with a form -->
...
<button id="close" type="button">Close</button>
...

note.en: Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 2.5.2 due to activating a control on the down-event (F101).

summary.en: Where practical, make the control’s text label and name match. The visual label for controls is a trigger for speech activation. People who operate with voice interaction use the visible labels in their commands.

examples.bad: <button id="sitesearch" aria-label="Find in this site">Go</button>
examples.good: Go to our Code of conduct

note.en: Good: Matching the accessible name to the visible label (G211). Bad: Failure due to the accessible name not containing the visible label text (F96).

summary.en: Don't rely solely on device motion to control page content. Content is not dependent on a user's ability to move a device. Some people cannot hold or move a device steadily.
For any action that involves dragging, provide a simple pointer alternative. Don’t rely on dragging for user actions. Some people cannot use a mouse to drag items.
Ensure targets meet a minimum size or have sufficient spacing around them. Make controls easier to activate. Some people with physical impairments cannot click small buttons that are close together.

examples.good:
1. previous
  2. 1
  3. 2
  4. 3
  5. 4
  6. 5
  7. next

note.en: Good: Using min-height and min-width on target container to ensure sufficient target spacing (C42).

summary.en: Indicate the predominant language on a page. Assistive technology can determine the language of a page. People using assistive technology get information in the correct language.

examples.good:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>document écrit en français</title>
</head>
<body>
  ... document écrit en français ...
</body>
</html>

note.en: Good: Using the language attribute on the HTML element (H57).

summary.en: Indicate when words are in a different language. Assistive technology can identify the languages used within a page. People using assistive technology get information in the correct language.
Do not change a user's context when items get focus. Content can be navigated more predictably. Content that behaves predictably is especially important to people with disabilities.

examples.bad: <input type="submit" onFocus="this.blur();">

note.en: Bad: Failure of Success Criteria 2.1.1, 2.4.7, 2.4.13, and 3.2.1 due to using script to remove focus when focus is received (F55).

summary.en: Forewarn users if their context will change based on their input. Content can be operated more predictably. Content that behaves predictably is especially important to people with disabilities.

examples.bad:
<form method="get" id="form1">
   <input type="text" name="text1" size="3" maxlength="3"> - 
   <input type="text" name="text2" size="3" maxlength="3"> - 
   <input type="text" name="text3" size="4" maxlength="4" onchange="form1.submit();">
 </form>
examples.good: Enter your email address to subscribe to our mailing list.

note.en: Good: Providing submit buttons (H32). Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 3.2.2 due to automatically submitting a form and presenting new content without prior warning when the last field in the form is given a value (F36).

summary.en: Consistently order navigation that repeats across multiple pages. Content can be navigated more predictably. Content that behaves predictably is especially important to people with disabilities.

examples.bad:
• Brazil
  • Canada
  • Germany
  • Poland

note.en: Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 3.2.3 due to presenting navigation links in a different relative order on different pages (F66).

summary.en: Identify repeating functions consistently. Actions are more predictable across pages. Consistently identified actions are especially important to people with disabilities.
Put help in the same place when it is on multiple pages. Make it easier to find help and support. People who need help can find it more easily if it's in the same place.
Provide descriptive notification of errors. Users know an error exists and what is wrong. Flagging errors helps people with reduced sight and cognitive disabilities resolve them.

note.en: Good: Using aria-invalid to Indicate An Error Field (ARIA21).

summary.en: Provide labels or instructions for inputs. Users know what information to enter. Everyone, especially those with cognitive disabilities, will know how to respond.

examples.good:
<label for="firstname">First name (required):</label> 
<input id="firstname" name="firstname" type="text">

note.en: Good: Indicating required form controls using label or legend (H90).

summary.en: Where errors are detected, suggest known ways to correct them. Users get suggestions on how to resolve errors. People can address errors faster and with reduced effort.

examples.good:
Error

Employee's Birth Date is after their hire date. Please verify the birth date and hire date.

note.en: Good: Using aria-alertdialog to Identify Errors (ARIA18).

title.fr: Prévention des erreurs (juridiques, financières, de données)

summary.en: Provide ways for users to confirm, correct, or reverse important submissions. Users can avoid submitting incorrect important information. People with disabilities may be more likely to make mistakes, or not notice them.

Don't ask for the same information twice in the same activity. Make it easier for users to complete multi-step processes. Some people with cognitive disabilities have difficulty remembering what they entered before.

Don't make people solve, recall, or transcribe something to log in. Make logins possible with less mental effort. Some people with cognitive disabilities cannot solve puzzles, memorize a username and password, or retype one-time passcodes.

note.en: Good: Providing properly marked up email and password inputs (H100).

summary.en: Give components correct names, roles, states, and values. People using assistive technology understand all components. Assistive technology only works well when code is done properly.

examples.bad: Include Signature
examples.good: Example Site

note.en: Good: Using HTML form controls and links (H91). Bad: Failure of Success Criterion 4.1.2 due to using script to make div or span a user interface control in HTML without providing a role for the control (F59).

summary.en: Let assistive technology notify users about status changes that don't take focus. Make users aware of important changes in content. People who do not see messages need to be informed about them.

examples.good:
Recent activity

  • 08:03 UserX logged off

note.en: Good: Using role=log to identify sequential information updates (ARIA23).
